h1: GEO vs SEO: what actually changes in the work
metaTitle: GEO vs SEO: What Actually Changes in the Work
metaDescription: The difference between GEO and SEO is smaller than the hype suggests. Here's what genuinely changes in the work, and the budget share worth moving now.
answer: GEO is SEO with a different scoring surface. Generative engines still retrieve from a search index, so crawling, content and links still decide whether you're eligible at all. What genuinely changes is format: self-contained answers, citable numbers, consistent entity data and comparison tables. Roughly 10–15% of a ₹75,000 retainer is worth reallocating.
takeaways: Retrieval runs on an index. If you're not indexed and ranking somewhere in the top results, you're not in the citation pool — so GEO cannot replace SEO, only sit on top of it.
Four deliverables genuinely change: **answer-first formatting**, **original statistics**, **comparison tables**, **entity consistency**. Everything else is the same job with new vocabulary.
There is no reliable rank tracker for generative answers. Anyone selling you a precise AI share-of-voice number is modelling, not measuring.
Move **10–15%** of the retainer, not 50%. Defunding technical work and links to chase citations is how you lose both.

sections.h2: What generative engines actually cite, and why
body: Strip the branding off AI Overviews, ChatGPT's browsing mode, Perplexity and Copilot and they share one shape: a query gets rewritten into several sub-queries, each hits a search index, a handful of pages come back, and the model writes an answer out of what it can extract from them. The citation is a receipt for that extraction.
That mechanic explains almost everything about which pages get picked. It isn't mystical and there's no new algorithm to reverse-engineer.

Cited pages share four properties: they were already retrievable for the sub-query, they hold a passage that answers it without the rest of the page, they say something specific enough to quote, and they name entities the model can resolve. A page ranking fifth that holds the answering paragraph beats the page ranking first that buries it.

callout.title: The uncomfortable part
callout.body: Getting cited is not the same as getting a click. On informational queries you can win the citation and lose the visit. That's a real trade, and it's why the measurement section of this page matters more than the tactics section.

body: Most GEO pitches are a re-skin of an SEO scope of work. Here's the line-by-line, so you can see which parts you'd genuinely be paying extra for.

sections.h2: Entity consistency is the one genuinely new discipline
body: The other three changes are formatting habits a good editor picks up in a week. Entity consistency is different work, and most teams have never done it.

A generative engine has to decide that the business named in a Bengaluru directory, the one quoted in a trade publication and the domain it just crawled are the same organisation. Everywhere your details disagree, that confidence drops — and a model unsure who you are will leave you out and cite someone unambiguous.
This is unglamorous audit work: one spreadsheet, every surface where your business is described, a column per fact that has to match.
bullets: **Legal and trading name** — one form, everywhere. "Pvt Ltd" in some places and not others is a real ambiguity, not pedantry.
**Category description.** If your site says "SEO agency", LinkedIn says "growth partner" and a directory says "web design company", you've described three businesses.
**Founders and named people** — same spellings, same roles, on an about page with `sameAs` pointing at their real profiles.
**Location and service area** — one address format, and an explicit statement of where you work.
**Pricing and claims.** If your site says ₹75,000/mo and an old press piece says ₹25,000, the model can't tell which is current.
**Organization schema on the homepage**, with `sameAs` for every profile you control. The cheapest disambiguation signal available.

callout.title: Where this bites hardest
callout.body: Businesses that rebranded, repriced or moved city in the last three years. The old facts are still sitting in directories and old coverage, and a model has no way to date them. Fixing that is often the highest-yield GEO work available, and it looks nothing like content marketing.

sections.h2: How to measure this when no rank tracker covers it
body: There's no rank tracker here, because there's no stable position-based result to track. Answers vary by user, session, phrasing and day. Three honest routes exist, each with a hole in it.
numbered: **Search Console, read for the signature.** Google folds AI Overview impressions and clicks into the standard performance report rather than splitting them out, so you can't isolate them. What you can watch is the pattern: impressions holding or rising on informational queries while CTR falls. That's a pattern, not proof — say so when you report it.

**GA4 referrals from assistant hostnames.** Traffic from `chatgpt.com`, `perplexity.ai`, `copilot.microsoft.com` and `gemini.google.com` arrives as referral. Small volumes, usually high intent. Build a custom channel group so it stops hiding inside "Referral" or "Unassigned".

**A manual prompt log.** Fix a panel of 25–30 prompts a real buyer would type. Run them monthly, same day, logged out, same engines. Record whether you were cited, which page, and who else was in the answer. Tedious, a sample rather than a census, and still the most truthful number here.

callout.title: The vendor test
callout.body: If an agency shows you a precise "AI visibility score" or a share-of-voice percentage, ask two questions: how many prompts is that sampled from, and were they run logged out? The answers are usually "a few dozen" and "we're not sure" — which is fine, as long as it's labelled as a sample instead of sold as a measurement.

sections.h2: The share of a ₹75,000 retainer worth reallocating
body: Here's our actual call, with the reasoning, because a number without reasoning is a guess in a nicer font. On a ₹75,000/month retainer we'd move roughly 10–15% of the effort — ₹8,000 to ₹11,000 worth of hours — and take it from specific places rather than shaving everything evenly.

bullets: **What we wouldn't defund:** technical health, indexing and links. Retrieval runs on an index. Fall out of it and you fall out of the answer.

**What we wouldn't buy:** a separate GEO retainer stacked on SEO. Same team, adjusted version of the same work. A second fee is a charge for vocabulary — our [AI search optimisation service](/services/ai-search-optimisation-services) sets out the real scope.
**When to move more than 15%:** research-heavy B2B, or categories where buyers ask assistants for shortlists. Move less if you sell an urgent local service.

sections.h2: The verdict, and what to do on Monday
body: Forced to pick one, pick SEO — not out of caution, but because GEO without indexing and rankings is a scope of work with no distribution attached. Every generative surface reads from a search index, and the index doesn't care what you call your discipline.
If you already rank well and you're watching CTR erode on informational queries, that's the moment GEO earns its 15%. Reformat before you write more. Then publish one number nobody else has.

Monday's list: take your top 20 pages by impressions, add a 40–60 word answer under every H2, fix Organization schema and `sameAs`, start the prompt log. A week of work, covering most of what GEO means in practice. Longer argument in [is generative engine optimisation real](/journal/is-generative-engine-optimization-real).

faqs.q: What is the difference between GEO and SEO?
faqs.a: SEO optimises for a ranked list of links. GEO optimises for a synthesised answer that cites a few sources. The plumbing is shared — generative engines retrieve from a search index — so the difference lands in formatting and entity clarity rather than in a separate discipline. Four deliverables genuinely change; the rest is the same work.

No, and it can't. Generative engines retrieve candidates from a search index before writing anything. If you're not crawlable, indexed and ranking somewhere in the retrievable set, you're not in the citation pool at all. GEO is a layer on top of SEO, not a substitute for it.

faqs.q: How do I get cited by ChatGPT or AI Overviews?
faqs.a: Rank for the sub-questions, then make the answer extractable. In practice: a self-contained 40–60 word answer under every H2, one specific number or definition worth quoting, a comparison table for "X vs Y" questions, and consistent entity data so the model knows who you are. There's no submission form and nobody can guarantee a citation.

Not yet. It's a proposed convention for pointing language models at a clean version of your content, and no major engine has committed to reading it. Adding one costs about twenty minutes, so it's not a bad bet — just don't let anyone bill it as a GEO strategy.

faqs.q: How much of my SEO budget should go to GEO?
faqs.a: Around 10–15% on a ₹75,000/month retainer, taken from article volume and generic outreach rather than from technical work or links. Research-heavy B2B categories can justify more. Urgent local services should spend less — those buyers aren't asking an assistant, they're tapping a phone number in the map pack.

faqs.q: Can I track my AI citations like keyword rankings?
faqs.a: Not reliably. Answers vary by user, phrasing and day, and Google folds AI Overview data into its standard Search Console reports rather than separating it. The honest method is a fixed panel of 25–30 prompts run monthly, logged out, with the results recorded by hand. Treat it as a sample, never as a census.

versus.verdict: If you're choosing where the next rupee goes, put it in SEO — generative engines retrieve from a search index, so an unindexed page can't be cited; only once you're already ranking does moving 10–15% of the retainer into GEO formatting pay.
